events.reason: Proteinuria and hematuria with red cell casts, edema, malar rash

reports.text: Specimen: kidney, left, percutaneous needle core biopsy under ultrasound guidance (both kidneys normal in size on the guiding ultrasound). Adequacy: adequate; cortex present with sufficient glomeruli for evaluation. Light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy reviewed together. Glomeruli show active lesions. No significant glomerulosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis or tubular atrophy.
reports.conclusion: Lupus nephritis, ISN/RPS class IV, with active lesions and no significant chronic damage.

documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL — NEPHROLOGY ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
Admitted: 06/30/2025
Referring: primary care (urgent)

Chief complaint: three weeks of fatigue, joint pain and leg swelling, with a new facial rash.

HPI: 33 year old woman with prior hydrochlorothiazide-induced photosensitivity (October 2024). For three weeks she has felt run down, with aching joints and swollen legs. She has also developed a red rash across both cheeks that gets worse with sun. No recent infections. No travel. Her PCP found blood, protein and casts in the urine last week and called us.

PMH: mild persistent asthma; seasonal allergic rhinitis; OCD; generalized anxiety disorder; migraine without aura; acne vulgaris. Hydrochlorothiazide photosensitivity 10/2024.
PSH: none.

Home medications:
- albuterol HFA 90 mcg: 1-2 puffs q4-6h PRN
- fluticasone propionate HFA 44 mcg, 2 puffs twice daily
- sertraline 100 mg daily
- sumatriptan 50 mg as needed (max 200 mg/day)
- hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily: STOPPED 10/2024 (photosensitivity)
She uses her albuterol inhaler only occasionally.

Allergies: seasonal pollens (tree, grass); hydrochlorothiazide (photosensitivity).

Family history: mother with SLE; father with asthma and seasonal allergies; sister with major depressive disorder.
Social: never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks per month; graphic designer.

Exam: BP 145/90, HR 86, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98% RA.
General: fatigued, no distress. Skin: erythematous malar rash. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no rub, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities: bilateral pitting edema to the shins. Joints: no synovitis.

Labs (6/30): urinalysis with protein and blood, red blood cell casts on microscopy. Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Albumin 2.8 g/dL. 24-hour urine protein 4.5 g. ANA positive.

Assessment: active urine sediment with heavy proteinuria, low albumin, edema and raised blood pressure, together with a photosensitive malar rash and arthralgia. Strong concern for lupus nephritis.

Plan: complement levels and anti-dsDNA sent. Kidney biopsy 7/1. Given the proteinuria and active sediment, IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily x 3 days started 6/30 after discussion with the patient. Daily weights, low salt diet.

ADDENDUM 07/01/2025 08:40: C3 low. C4 low. Anti-dsDNA positive. With the positive ANA, this is systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with a lupus nephritis flare. Rheumatology aware. Biopsy proceeding today.

Nephrology

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL — DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 06/30/2025   Discharged: 07/03/2025
Service: Nephrology

Principal diagnosis: systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with lupus nephritis flare, ISN/RPS class IV.

Hospital course:
Admitted from clinic with protein, blood and red cell casts in the urine, 24-hour protein 4.5 g, creatinine 1.2, albumin 2.8, BP 145/90, leg edema and a photosensitive malar rash. ANA and anti-dsDNA positive, C3 and C4 low.
Received IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days (6/30 to 7/2).
Ultrasound-guided left kidney biopsy 7/1, uncomplicated: class IV lupus nephritis with active lesions, no significant chronic damage.
BP improving at discharge (132/84 this morning). Edema slowly improving.

Discharge medications:
NEW
- prednisone 40 mg by mouth daily
- mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg by mouth twice daily
- hydroxychloroquine 200 mg by mouth daily
- losartan 25 mg by mouth daily (proteinuria and blood pressure)
CONTINUE
- albuterol HFA as needed; fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily; sertraline 100 mg daily; sumatriptan 50 mg as needed
Allergies: seasonal pollens; hydrochlorothiazide (photosensitivity).

Counselling: mycophenolate and losartan can harm a pregnancy and must not be taken if pregnant; she reports reliable contraception. Sun protection. Infection precautions on immunosuppression.

Follow-up:
- Outside nephrology clinic in 2 to 3 months, labs before.
- Outside rheumatology new-patient visit, being scheduled.
- PCP within 1 week.

Nephrology

documents.title: Rheumatology consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
RHEUMATOLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/12/2025
Referred from: inpatient nephrology / primary care

Ms. Williams is a 33 year old woman hospitalized 6/30 to 7/3/2025 with a lupus nephritis flare as the presenting manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus. Kidney biopsy showed ISN/RPS class IV with active lesions and no significant chronic damage. She received three days of IV methylprednisolone and was discharged on prednisone 40 mg daily, mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg twice daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily and losartan 25 mg daily.

She describes the photosensitive rash across the cheeks and aching joints that came on in the weeks before admission, both now easing. Swelling in the legs is better. She is tolerating the mycophenolate. Mother has SLE.

Allergies: hydrochlorothiazide (photosensitivity); seasonal pollens.

Exam: BP 123/74, HR 80, weight 66.6 kg. Faint residual malar erythema. Mouth without ulcers. Joints without synovitis today. Heart and lungs normal.

Assessment: Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus nephritis (class IV), malar rash and arthralgia, responding to induction.

Plan:
1. Continue mycophenolate 1000 mg twice daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily and losartan 25 mg daily.
2. Begin prednisone taper today; written schedule given to the patient. Nephrology is aware.
3. Baseline hydroxychloroquine eye exam (referral already placed by her PCP).
4. Strict sun protection.
5. Return in about 5 months, sooner for a flare.

Rheumatology
